title: Baptist History and Distinctives
summary: Where Baptists came from, what they believe and why: from the English Separatists to the Nigerian Baptist Convention, and the convictions that mark Baptist churches.
description: Baptists are among the largest Protestant families in the world and in Nigeria. This course traces Baptist origins in seventeenth-century England, the struggle for religious liberty, the spread of Baptists to America and through missions to Nigeria, and the key Baptist distinctives: the authority of Scripture, believer's baptism by immersion, a regenerate church, congregational government, the priesthood of all believers, and religious liberty. It also notes how other traditions view these convictions.
objectives: Trace the origins and growth of Baptists
Explain the Baptist commitment to religious liberty
Describe the beginnings and growth of Baptist work in Nigeria
Explain the main Baptist distinctives with their biblical basis
Relate Baptist convictions respectfully to other traditions
outcomes: Explain the roles of Smyth, Helwys and Roger Williams
Describe the work of Bowen and the founding of the Nigerian Baptist Convention
Show where Baptists agree and differ with other evangelicals

modules.title: Baptist Beginnings
modules.intro: Baptists emerged from English Puritan and Separatist movements in the early 1600s. This week we study their origins.

lessons.title: From Separatists to Baptists
lessons.body:
Some English Puritans concluded the Church of England could not be reformed from within and formed separate congregations. Persecuted, a group led by **John Smyth** and **Thomas Helwys** fled to Amsterdam.

Studying the New Testament, Smyth concluded in **1609** that baptism belongs to professing believers, not infants. The congregation was reconstituted on believer's baptism, often counted as the first Baptist church.

In **1612** Helwys returned to England and founded the first Baptist church on English soil at Spitalfields, near London. Baptists believed they were recovering the New Testament pattern: "Then they that gladly received his word were baptized" (Acts 2:41).

lessons.title: General and Particular Baptists
lessons.body:
Early English Baptists formed two main streams:

- **General Baptists** (from Helwys) held that Christ died for all people generally: an Arminian view.
- **Particular Baptists** (from the 1630s) held that Christ died particularly for the elect: a Calvinist view. They began practising baptism by immersion and issued the **London Baptist Confession** (1644) and the **Second London Confession** (1689).

Great Particular Baptists included **John Bunyan**, author of *The Pilgrim's Progress*, **William Carey** and later **Charles Spurgeon**. Many Baptist churches today, including in Nigeria, hold positions between or across these streams.

lessons.title: A plea for liberty
lessons.body:
Helwys wrote *A Short Declaration of the Mystery of Iniquity* (1612), one of the first pleas in English for full religious freedom. He argued that the king has authority over bodies, not over consciences, and that people of every faith should be free to worship. He died in prison.

Baptists suffered fines, prison and death for their convictions, yet they defended freedom of conscience not only for themselves but for all people.

This conviction rests on Scripture: faith cannot be forced (2 Corinthians 5:11, 20); each person will give account to God (Romans 14:12); and Christ's kingdom is "not of this world" (John 18:36).

modules.title: Baptists Spread Worldwide
modules.intro: Baptists grew in America and spread worldwide through missions. This week we follow their path to Nigeria.

lessons.title: Baptists in America
lessons.body:
**Roger Williams**, banished from Massachusetts for his views on religious liberty, founded Providence, Rhode Island, as a haven for freedom of conscience. There in 1638-1639 he helped form the first Baptist church in America.

Baptists grew rapidly during the Great Awakenings, especially among ordinary people and enslaved Africans. They campaigned for religious liberty in the new United States.

In 1845 Baptists in the southern states formed the **Southern Baptist Convention**, sadly in a dispute connected with slavery. The SBC later apologised (1995) for its support of slavery and racism. Its Foreign Mission Board sent missionaries around the world, including to Nigeria.

lessons.title: Baptist beginnings in Nigeria
lessons.body:
In **1850** the Southern Baptist missionary **Thomas Jefferson Bowen** arrived at Badagry and travelled into Yorubaland, working at Ijaye and Ogbomoso. He studied the Yoruba language and wrote a Yoruba grammar and dictionary.

Work was hindered by wars, disease and the American Civil War, but continued through missionaries and faithful Nigerian believers. Churches grew in Lagos, Abeokuta, Ogbomoso, Oyo and beyond.

In 1888 some members of the Lagos church formed the **Native Baptist Church**, an early African-led church, reflecting the desire for Nigerian leadership.

lessons.title: The Nigerian Baptist Convention
lessons.body:
In **1914** Baptist churches formed what became the **Nigerian Baptist Convention**, now one of the largest Baptist bodies in the world, with churches across Nigeria.

The Nigerian Baptist Theological Seminary in Ogbomoso, founded in 1898, has trained generations of pastors. Baptists also founded schools, hospitals (such as the Baptist Medical Centre in Ogbomoso) and colleges that served the nation.

Today the Convention sends its own missionaries in Nigeria and abroad. Its churches cooperate in associations and conferences while each local church keeps its autonomy, in line with Baptist principles.

modules.title: Baptist Distinctives (1)
modules.intro: What makes a church Baptist? This week we study the first set of Baptist distinctives.

lessons.title: The authority of Scripture
lessons.body:
Baptists often summarise their convictions with the acrostic **BAPTIST**. The first is **B: Biblical authority**.

Baptists hold that the Bible alone is the final authority for faith and practice, above creeds, traditions, councils or leaders. "All scripture is given by inspiration of God" (2 Timothy 3:16). Baptist confessions are valued as summaries, not as authorities over Scripture.

This is why Baptists insisted on believer's baptism and congregational government: they sought to follow the New Testament pattern rather than tradition, as Jesus rebuked those "making the word of God of none effect through your tradition" (Mark 7:13).

lessons.title: Autonomy and congregational government
lessons.body:
**A: Autonomy of the local church.** Each local church is self-governing under Christ, choosing its own leaders, receiving members and exercising discipline. Baptists point to the church choosing the seven (Acts 6:3-5), the whole church disciplining (Matthew 18:17; 1 Corinthians 5:4) and letters addressed to whole congregations.

Autonomy is not isolation. Baptist churches cooperate voluntarily in associations and conventions for mission, education and fellowship, as the New Testament churches cooperated (2 Corinthians 8:1-4).

Other traditions, such as Anglicans, Methodists and many Pentecostal churches, have bishops or overseers with authority over many churches.

lessons.title: The priesthood of all believers
lessons.body:
**P: Priesthood of all believers.** Every believer has direct access to God through Christ, the one Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), and is part of "an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices" (1 Peter 2:5, 9). No earthly priest is needed to stand between a believer and God.

This means every member may read and interpret Scripture, pray directly to God, minister to others, and share in church decisions. It does not deny the value of pastors, who are gifts to equip the saints (Ephesians 4:11-12).

This conviction was shared with the Reformers and is held by most Protestants, though Baptists stress its implications for church life.

modules.title: Baptist Distinctives (2)
modules.intro: This week we study the remaining distinctives and how Baptists relate to other Christians.

lessons.title: Two ordinances and a regenerate church
lessons.body:
**T: Two ordinances.** Baptists observe baptism and the Lord's Supper as ordinances commanded by Christ, symbols of the gospel rather than means of saving grace. Baptism is for professing believers, by **immersion**, picturing burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:3-4).

**S: Saved (regenerate) church membership.** Church membership is for those who give credible evidence of new birth and have been baptized as believers. The New Testament churches were made up of "saints" and "faithful brethren" (Colossians 1:2), and "the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved" (Acts 2:47).

This is why Baptists do not baptize infants: membership follows personal faith.

lessons.title: Soul liberty and two offices
lessons.body:
**I: Individual soul liberty.** Every person is responsible directly to God and must be free to believe without coercion by church or state. Baptists hold to **separation of church and state**: the state should neither control the church nor favour one religion, and the church should not use state power to force faith. Faith must be voluntary (Joshua 24:15).

**T: Two offices.** The New Testament names two ongoing church offices: **pastors** (elders, bishops) and **deacons** (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3).

These convictions, held together, describe the Baptist way of being church.

lessons.title: Baptists among other Christians
lessons.body:
Baptists share the core gospel with all evangelical Christians: the Trinity, Christ's deity and atonement, salvation by grace through faith, and the authority of Scripture.

They differ with others on secondary matters: infant baptism (Anglican, Methodist, Presbyterian, Catholic), church government (episcopal and presbyterian churches), and sometimes on Spirit baptism and gifts (Pentecostals). Baptists themselves vary: some are Calvinist, others Arminian; some continuationist, others cessationist.

Baptists should hold their convictions firmly but humbly, "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Ephesians 4:3), cooperating with other believers in the gospel.
